draft.title: Persuasive writing craft
card: A persuasive piece takes a clear position and holds to it. The reader should know early what the writer wants them to believe or do.
Evidence, such as facts, examples and expert views, supports the position. Without it, the piece is only opinion.
uses logic and evidence to show the position makes sense.
uses vivid detail or personal stories to make the reader care. Strong pieces often blend both, in a voice the reader can trust.
draft.remember: Persuade with a clear position, evidence, reason and feeling, and a trusted voice. Use rhetorical questions and repetition sparingly.

a.q: Which sentence from a speech about school start times is an appeal to reason?
opts: Studies of teenage sleep show later starts lift test scores
Picture a tired student, head down, missing the lesson
We owe our children a morning they can face with hope
Every parent has watched a weary teenager stumble from bed
a.why: The first option points to evidence and draws a logical conclusion from it. The others are tempting because they are strong, but they work mainly on feeling through imagery and emotion.
a.clue: Which one relies on evidence rather than emotion?

b.q: Mia drafts a speech urging her council to build a skate park. Which change would best improve its persuasive craft?
opts: Add local injury figures and a short story from one skater
Open every paragraph with a different rhetorical question
Repeat the phrase 'build it now' at the end of each sentence
Remove her own position so the speech sounds neutral
b.why: Figures give reason and a story gives feeling, so the piece uses both appeals. Heavy questions or repetition would be overuse, since they work best sparingly. Hiding her position would weaken the piece, which needs a clear stance.
b.clue: Look for the choice that adds both reason and feeling.

a.best: Studies of teenage sleep show later starts lift test scores

b.best: Add local injury figures and a short story from one skater

proposal.title: Persuasive writing craft
card: A persuasive piece takes a clear position early and holds to it. A fair, confident voice helps the reader trust the writer.
Evidence, such as facts, examples and expert views, supports the position. Without it, the piece is only opinion.
An appeal to reason uses logic and evidence to show the position makes sense. An appeal to feeling uses vivid detail or personal stories to make the reader care. Strong pieces often blend both.
Rhetorical questions and repetition can add force. Used too often, they start to feel like tricks and can weaken the reader's trust.
proposal.remember: Persuasion blends evidence, reason and feeling in a trusted voice, with devices used sparingly.
